overview: This 203-page file documents the transformation of Japan’s press from a centralized instrument of wartime control into a regulated but increasingly pluralistic institution under the Allied Occupation. Its 22 documents include an OSS analysis of wartime censorship, SCAP newspaper statistics, an extensive nationwide directory of publishers, a detailed historical and organizational survey of news agencies, and diplomatic correspondence concerning information requests, wire-service payments, newspaper mergers, Press Code enforcement, circulation, and postwar press policy. Although the file title gives 1945 as its date range, the contents extend through 1949 and collectively trace both the structure of the Japanese publishing industry and the political project of press democratization.
interest: The file is especially useful because it combines policy analysis with unusually detailed empirical records, including circulation figures, staffing and equipment statistics, publisher addresses, representatives, specialties, and news-agency directories. The extended survey of news agencies makes it possible to follow the institutional transition from Domei’s wartime monopoly to the postwar system centered on Kyodo, Jiji, and numerous specialized services. Documents on Press Code prosecutions and MacArthur’s celebration of a “free press” also expose the tension between occupation censorship and official claims of democratization, while the shipment of Tokyo newspapers to Japanese communities in Brazil and Peru adds a distinctive transnational dimension.
